1.pericope_label: these be the words: place, hearers, and the eleven days

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the titles of the book and judge it a compendium of the whole law rather than a recapitulation; Ellicott works out the geography of the opening verse, reading the plain as the Arabah and the five names as two groups that mark the line of march from Sinai to Kadesh.
Gill denies that the whole nation could have been addressed at once without a miracle and takes the audience to be its representatives.
Henry sets the discourse in the plain of Moab on the eve of a war, and notes that Moses speaks of duty rather than strategy; he hears the reproach in the eleven days.
Clarke denies that the opening phrase settles which side of Jordan is meant or that the Red Sea is named at all, and reports the Saxon name for the book.

outliers: Clarke holds that the first five verses are not the work of Moses but were added later, probably by Joshua or Ezra.
themes: these be the words which Moses spake unto all Israel
eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea
between Paran and Tophel

3.pericope_label: the date, the victories, and the law declared

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the date significant, the lawgiving being complete and Sihon and Og already fallen, so that the victories lay Israel under obligation; Ellicott hears a reproach in the opening conjunction and argues from the rare verb that Moses here began to put his discourses into writing.

Calvin explains the need for a second exposition — brevity is obscurity to a slow-hearted people — and calls the renewal within sight of the land an extraordinary indulgence to a new generation; Gill weighs whether Moses speaks of himself in the third person.
Clarke reads the fortieth year as a season of bereavement and measures the whole book at five weeks; Wesley takes the rehearsal as commanded, and so as a legacy left to the church.

themes: in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day
after he had slain Sihon and Og
began Moses to declare this law

6.pericope_label: ye have dwelt long enough in this mount

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read both halves of the command as loaded — the covenant title presupposing Sinai, and the dismissal implying that the purpose of Horeb was answered — and admit candidly that this word is not found in this form in the earlier history; Ellicott calls the year at the mountain the period of organisation.

Calvin insists that a sign was not thought enough, God speaking as well as lifting the cloud, and notes that the command is framed to make the journey look easy to an indolent people; Gill identifies Horeb with Sinai.
Henry takes the departure as a mercy: God brought them there to humble them, and knows when his people have dwelt long enough in affliction of mind.

Clarke measures the stay at nearly a year and reads the list of places as a boundary, noting that Solomon reigned to exactly that extent; Wesley keeps to the plain sense of the land set before their faces.

themes: turn you, and take your journey
behold, I have set the land before you
the land which the LORD sware unto your fathers

9.pericope_label: I am not able to bear you myself alone

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the prayer as a guard against misreading the complaint, and take the burden to be the nation itself pressing on his shoulders; Ellicott notes that the word for cumbrance occurs in only one other place and hears the living speaker in the parenthesis.

Calvin defines the three qualifications as acuteness, discretion and tried experience, and fastens on the election of the judges by the votes of the people as the most desirable kind of liberty; Gill reads the prayer as proof that Moses did not envy the increase.
Henry defends a prayer inserted in a discourse, presses the size of the request, and contrasts an increase envied under Pharaoh with the same increase prayed for under Moses.
Clarke defends the comparison with the stars arithmetically against the charge of hyperbole; Wesley divides the burden into ruling a perverse people and settling their quarrels.

outliers: Clarke counts the stars visible to the naked eye at about three thousand and sets them against six hundred thousand fighting men, to defend the comparison as literal rather than rhetorical.
themes: I am not able to bear you myself alone
the LORD make you a thousand times so many more
take you wise men, and understanding, and known

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the judgment as appointed by God and administered in his name; Ellicott calls the charge an expansion of Jethro's counsel and finds Paul's account of the magistrate an expansion of this one sentence.

Calvin explains why the charge is absent from the earlier account, and holds that the commoner failure is not contempt of the poor but fear of the powerful, so that what is required of a judge is magnanimity; Gill lists the distinctions that must not count.

Clarke states the two ways of failing — the bold countenance and the abject look — and sums the reason in a line; Wesley reports that some Greek lawgivers had their judges give sentence in the dark, and marks the inclusion of the stranger.

themes: judge righteously between every man and his brother
ye shall not respect persons in judgment
the judgment is God's

schools.summary: Ellicott shows that the request came from the people first and that asking to be told the route was taking the guidance of the march into their own hands — an act of unbelief, set against the campaigns of Joshua in which no step was taken without divine direction; Keil and Delitzsch identify the desert and hold that the summons to go up is implied in the older account.
Gill notes that the proposal pleased Moses well, since he took it for prudent and did not suspect fear and distrust behind it.
Henry lays the sending on the people, contrasts human policy with divine wisdom — they must needs light a candle to the sun — and observes that even unbelievers granted the land was good.

debates.question: Who initiated the sending of the spies?
positions: Numbers has the Lord directing it; Deuteronomy has the people asking first
Henry and Ellicott resolve it in sequence — the people proposed, Moses referred it, God permitted; Keil and Delitzsch hold the summons is implied in the older narrative

themes: that great and terrible wilderness
we will send men before us
it is a good land which the LORD our God doth give us

26.pericope_label: the refusal, and the appeal that failed

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the verb for discouraging as making the heart flow away, defend the walls reaching to heaven as a record of the impression received, and read the participle for unbelief as a settled condition; Ellicott calls the charge that God hated them stronger than anything in the earlier account, and points out the irony of a people reminded that God went before them when they had already sent men to go before them.

Calvin works out the perversity of construing a deliverance into hatred, revises his earlier impression of the spies, and notes the emphasis on what was done before their own eyes; Gill places the murmuring in the tents before it became public.

Clarke supplies a traveller's note on high walls without gates and reports the Targum's "the Word of the Lord shall fight for you"; Wesley glosses the comparison of the peoples as one of number, strength and valour.

themes: because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth
the cities are great and walled up to heaven
as a man doth bear his son, so the LORD bare thee

fidelity.note: The opening of the third paragraph calls the charge that God hated them "the worst sentence in the chapter, and both Ellicott and Calvin say so". Ellicott does say it is stronger than any complaint recorded in Numbers; Calvin condemns it as malignant ingratitude but does not rank it. The superlative is the summary's.

34.pericope_label: the oath, and the exceptions to it

schools.summary: Ellicott arranges the exceptions — Caleb alone among the people, Joshua apart among the leaders — and explains why the rejection of Moses, an event of the fortieth year, is folded in here: the reason in both cases was unbelief; Keil and Delitzsch gloss standing before Moses as being in his service.

Calvin defends the phrase for your sakes as reproof rather than evasion, leaves the preference of Joshua over Caleb with God, and uses the limit of the pardon to argue that everyone past the years of reason was an accomplice; Gill notes that the sentence covered the whole body that credited the report.
Clarke states that God could not have been just and not been angry; Wesley reads Caleb as including Joshua by implication.

outliers: Calvin blocks the inference that this verse frees infants from original sin, distinguishing children from those who consciously provoked God without denying the root of corruption in them.
themes: there shall not one of these men see that good land
save Caleb the son of Jephunneh
your little ones, which ye said should be a prey

41.pericope_label: the presumptuous attack, and the defeat at Hormah

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the emphatic we of this verse beside the we of the earlier complaint and calls the change one from cowardice to presumption rather than from unbelief to faith; he takes the incidental mention of bees as evidence of the writer's own knowledge, and notes that the weeping is not recorded in the earlier account at all.

Calvin denies that this was true repentance, marks that God withdrew his assistance as well as forbidding the battle, treats the weeping as evidence the people supplied against themselves, and prefers to read the closing phrase as an indefinite long time; Gill dates the prohibition to the moment they were armed and moving.
Clarke and Wesley both work at the simile of the bees, the one for irresistible numbers, the other for the fury of a provoked hive.

debates.question: How long did they abide in Kadesh?
positions: another forty days, on one reading of the repeated phrase
Calvin prefers an indefinite long time, the phrase being a Hebrew form of repetition

themes: we have sinned against the LORD, we will go up and fight
go not up, neither fight; for I am not among you
chased you, as bees do
